title: Current Assets and Non-current Assets
subtitle: Classifying assets by liquidity
openingQuestion: Which of the following is a Non-current Asset?
explanation: Assets are split by a single question: will it turn into cash within twelve months. Current covers cash, receivables, inventory; non-current covers plant, equipment, intangible assets, and long-term investments. The mix between the two groups says a lot about the business model: a business heavy in long-term assets struggles to adapt when demand drops, while an asset-light business is more flexible but also faces lower barriers to entry.

diagram.label: Will this asset turn into cash within 12 months?
Yes: current asset - cash, receivables, inventory
No: non-current asset - plant, equipment, intangibles
The mix between the two decides how flexible the business is

realWorldExample.description: Hoa Phat is a textbook example of a Balance Sheet leaning heavily toward Non-current Assets: integrated steel complexes such as Dung Quat represent a PP&E block (plants, blast furnaces, production lines) worth tens of trillions of VND, taking up a very large share of total assets. By contrast, Hoa Phat's Current Assets consist of iron-ore and coke inventory, finished steel, and receivables from distributors. A high share of Non-current Assets reflects the nature of capital-intensive manufacturing - it requires large upfront investment and a long payback period.

quiz.question: What is a Current Asset?
options: The single highest-value asset category on the entire balance sheet, usually plant and equipment
An asset that will turn into cash within 12 months: cash, receivables, inventory
A fixed asset used for production, depreciated gradually over the years
An asset the company is pledging to a bank for a short-term loan
quiz.explanation: Current Assets = will be used/sold/consumed within 1 year. Includes: Cash, Receivables, Inventory.

quiz.question: What is a Non-current Asset?
options: A low-value, insignificant asset that doesn't need separate tracking
A loss-making or impaired asset awaiting removal from the balance sheet
An asset held for longer than 12 months: real estate, machinery, patents
An asset not owned by the company but still being used
quiz.explanation: Non-current Assets = long-term assets = held for >1 year to generate future revenue.

quiz.question: Among Current Assets, which one has the highest liquidity?
options: Inventory - goods can always be sold right away
Prepaid expenses - already paid, so they can be reclaimed at any time
Receivables - customers owe payment, so it's treated almost like cash
Cash - needs no conversion, usable immediately
quiz.explanation: Liquidity = how long it takes to become cash. Cash = 0 days, Receivables = 30-60 days, Inventory = 60-90+ days.

quiz.question: Working Capital = ?
options: Current Assets - Current Liabilities = ability to pay short-term debt
Current Assets + Current Liabilities = total short-term funding for the period
Revenue - COGS = gross profit used to fund operations
Charter capital divided by headcount, i.e. capital per employee
quiz.explanation: WC = current assets minus current liabilities. Positive = good (can pay debt). Negative = dangerous.

quiz.question: If Working Capital falls, what could be the cause?
options: Rising revenue, since higher revenue always pulls working capital down
Inventory or receivables growing fast, current liabilities rising, or cash falling
Rising profit, since profit is always recorded straight into the current liabilities a company owes
Paying a stock dividend, which reduces equity accordingly
quiz.explanation: Falling WC means a weaker ability to pay short-term debt. Check: is cash flow OK, is inventory stuck, are receivables not overdue.

quiz.question: Current Ratio = ?
options: Current Assets × 2, a double safety buffer for debt coming due
Current Assets - Revenue, the portion of assets not created by revenue
Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities - above 1 is good, below 1 is risky
Current Liabilities ÷ Current Assets - the higher, the safer
quiz.explanation: CR = current assets / current liabilities. A CR of 1.5 means 1.5 dong of assets against 1 dong of debt, a 50% buffer.

quiz.question: Is Inventory a current or non-current asset?
options: Non-current - inventory is an asset the company holds for long-term production
Intangible - because its value depends on demand
Fixed - inventory must always be maintained at some minimum level
Current - most inventory is sold within less than a year
quiz.explanation: Inventory = goods awaiting sale. Usually sold within a month/quarter = current. Exceptions: vintage wine, real estate.

quiz.question: Why distinguish Current from Non-current Assets?
options: To assess liquidity: Current will soon become cash, Non-current is used long-term
Because accounting standards require it, with no other analytical meaning
Because only Current Assets count toward a company's total assets
Because Non-current Assets aren't depreciated, so they need separate lines
quiz.explanation: Current Assets are the short-term liquidity buffer. Non-current is the real long-term capital that generates future cash flow.

quiz.question: If a company has a Current Ratio of 0.8 (Current Liabilities > Current Assets), what does that signal?
options: Normal - most businesses sit around 0.8
Dangerous - not enough current assets to cover current liabilities
Very good - a ratio below 1 shows the company is using capital very efficiently
No effect, since the Current Ratio is only a formal accounting metric
quiz.explanation: CR < 1 = insolvency risk. Without improvement, the company may default on its debt.

quiz.question: Between Cash Ratio (Cash ÷ Current Liabilities) and Current Ratio, which is more conservative?
options: Current Ratio - since it combines all three types of current asset
They're equal, since both use Current Liabilities as the denominator
Cash Ratio - it counts only cash, ignoring receivables and inventory
They can't be compared, since the two ratios measure completely different things
quiz.explanation: Cash Ratio is ultra-conservative. Current Ratio is more conservative than the Acid-Test Ratio is aggressive. Acid-Test sits in between. Pick based on your risk tolerance.

quiz.question: When does Goodwill appear on a company's Balance Sheet, and why doesn't it appear naturally for a company that grew its brand entirely in-house?
options: When the company achieves consistently high profit for many years, the brand itself gets recognised
Every company automatically gains goodwill after 5 stable years of operation
When a company builds a strong brand itself, its value is revalued annually
Only when a company acquires another business for more than its net asset value
quiz.explanation: Goodwill only arises from M&A: Goodwill = Purchase Price − the fair value of the acquired company's net assets. This is why a company that built its own strong brand internally (like Google or Vinamilk) carries no huge goodwill on its books, even though its real brand value is very large.

keyTakeaways: Current assets: cash, AR, inventory - liquid within 1 year
The asset mix affects liquidity and risk

practicePrompt.question: A company has: cash 100 billion, receivables 50 billion, inventory 80 billion, a production plant worth 500 billion, and patents worth 30 billion. Which items are classified as current assets?
options: Only the 100 billion of cash is classified as a current asset; everything else is a non-current asset
Cash, receivables and inventory - that is 100 + 50 + 80 = 230 billion - all convertible within a year
All five items are classified as current assets, because the company owns and controls all of them
The production plant and patents are the current assets, since they keep generating value for the company continuously
practicePrompt.explanation: Current assets consist of cash, AR, and inventory - assets that can turn into cash or be consumed within 1 year (230 billion). Non-current consists of PP&E (the plant) and intangibles (the patents) - which deliver benefit over many years.

summary.keyIdea: Current assets: cash, AR, inventory - liquid within 1 year
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Classify a company's assets by liquidity
application.message: Open a company's Balance Sheet, underline the lines that belong to Current Assets and circle the lines that belong to Non-current Assets, then calculate each group's share of total assets.
application.secondary: A high share of long-term assets usually comes with a more capital-intensive business model.

sections.text: Not every asset carries the same 'value' in terms of liquidity. The Balance Sheet splits assets into two broad groups based on one criterion: will this asset turn into cash within the next 12 months.

Current Assets are assets expected to turn into cash, be sold, or be consumed within 12 months, including: Cash & Cash Equivalents, Accounts Receivable (AR), Inventory, and short-term investments. This group is usually listed in decreasing order of liquidity, starting from cash.

Non-current Assets are assets a company holds and uses for many years, not expected to be sold in the short term: PP&E - Property, Plant & Equipment (land, buildings, machinery), Intangible Assets (patents, brands, software), Goodwill (arising from M&A), and long-term investments.
Goodwill: a special kind of intangible asset

Goodwill arises when a company acquires another business for more than the fair value of the target's net assets - that gap reflects expectations about brand, loyal customers, or synergy from the deal. Goodwill isn't amortised periodically like PP&E, but it must be tested for impairment every year - if the M&A deal underperforms, the company must write down Goodwill, causing a large loss on the P&L.

items: Current Assets: Cash, AR, Inventory - turn into cash within 12 months.
Non-current Assets: PP&E, Intangibles, Goodwill - held long-term.
The Current/Non-current Assets mix reflects the industry: retail usually has a higher share of Current Assets, heavy manufacturing tends to lean Non-current.
Large Goodwill carries impairment risk if the M&A deal doesn't perform as expected.

left.label: High share of Current Assets
left.text: Common in retail and trading - assets are mostly cash, inventory, and receivables, giving better liquidity.

right.label: High share of Non-current Assets
right.text: Common in manufacturing, infrastructure, and real estate - requiring large upfront investment with a slower payback.
